posts.title: The Discipline of the Tasting Spoon
posts.excerpt: On their first morning inside our Veerkade teaching kitchens, every student receives a stainless steel tasting spoon that defines their daily standard of craft.
posts.content:
When Saji Culinary School opened its doors at Veerkade 18 in 2011, co-founders Marta Ilić and Owen Achterberg chose an old ship's-chandler warehouse along the canal for a deliberate purpose. They wanted high ceilings, wide brick walls, and concrete floors that could endure the rigorous demands of real kitchen production. Yet amid the heavy stainless steel ranges, walk-in coolers, and marble pastry tables, the most important tool they introduced to their students was remarkably small. It was a single, slender stainless steel tasting spoon—what in Japanese is called a saji. On day one of the forty-week Professional Cook Diploma, every student pulls this spoon from their new kit and slips it into their jacket sleeve pocket. There it remains through every station, sauce reduction, and lunch service.

The philosophy behind the spoon is straightforward: technique is meaningless if the cook does not understand flavor. In culinary education, students often spend hours obsessing over knife angles, uniform brunoise cuts, or the gloss of a pan sauce without ever stopping to taste what they have made. At Saji, an instructor will not evaluate a student's station until the cook has tasted the pot themselves. Whether reducing a brown stock with Lucía Ferrer in Term II, balancing acidity in a vinaigrette with Priya Raman, or simmering fruit compote with Owen Achterberg in Term III, the tasting spoon is dipped, evaluated, and washed continuously. Tasting trains the palate to detect missing salt, excessive acid, or subtle bitterness before food reaches the pass.

That sensory vigilance becomes urgent when the clock strikes 11:30. At Saji, students do not cook for abstract theory; they cook for forty real guests who fill the dining room of The Pass from Tuesday through Friday between 12:00 and 13:30. A three-course menu priced at €24 requires discipline and speed. Plates must leave the hot line hot, seasoned, and pristine. When tickets print and orders echo across the expediter station, there is no time to guess. Chef-instructor Marta Ilić stands at the pass with her own spoon, tasting alongside the student cooks. If a beurre blanc lacks brightness or a vegetable reduction requires another pinch of salt, the adjustment must happen instantly before plating begins.

This standard carries into the afternoon debrief at 14:00. Once the kitchen is scrubbed, counters bleached, and walk-in coolers organised, the cohort of twenty-four gathers around the demonstration bench. Instructors review ticket pacing, waste percentages, and plate consistency. Every victory and error is discussed openly. The debrief reinforces the reality that great cooks are not born of sudden inspiration, but built through deliberate daily repetition from 06:30 deliveries to 15:00 clean-down.

By the time students enter Term IV and prepare for six weeks in one of our thirty partner kitchens, the tasting spoon has become second nature. Whether our graduates step into hotel kitchens like Jonas Weber, artisanal bakeries like Aisha Bello, or neighbourhood bistros like Tomás Ortega, they carry the same habit into commercial lines. A cook who tastes constantly is a cook who respects their ingredients, their brigade, and the diner seated in the room.

posts.title: Open kitchen on the first Saturday of the month
posts.excerpt: Tour the kitchens, watch a class and meet the chef-instructors.
posts.content:
On the first Saturday of every month the teaching kitchens at Veerkade 18 are open from 10:00 to 13:00. You can walk the line, watch a technique class in progress and ask the chef-instructors how a training day is run.

Entry is free and no booking is needed. Bring questions about the diploma, the pastry and bread certificate or the evening courses; the admissions office is open the same morning.

posts.title: Applications for the February intake close on 1 December
posts.excerpt: Twenty-four places, one trial day and an interview with a chef-instructor.
posts.content:
The February intake has 24 places. Applications close on 1 December. After you apply online you are invited to a kitchen trial day (€60), then to an interview with a chef-instructor, and offers go out in the weeks that follow.

The September intake follows the same steps with a deadline of 1 June. No prior kitchen work is required; you need to be 17 or older.

posts.title: The Pass changes its lunch menu
posts.excerpt: A new three-course lunch written and cooked by the current Term IV cooks.
posts.content:
The student restaurant starts its autumn lunch this week. The menu is written by the Term IV cooks and tasted by their instructors before it goes on: a seasonal starter, a main and a dessert from the pastry bench.

Lunch is served Tuesday to Friday from 12:00 to 13:30. Three courses are €24, two courses €19. Tables can be booked by email or phone.

posts.title: Term IV placements begin in November
posts.excerpt: Six weeks in one of our 30 partner kitchens.
posts.content:
Every Term IV student spends six weeks in one of our 30 partner kitchens: hotel kitchens, bistros, bakeries, catering and hospital or school kitchens. Placements are agreed with each cook and the instructor who leads the term.

Students return for the final two weeks to cost and write the menu they present at the end of the diploma.

posts.title: Evening course: stocks and sauces, six evenings
posts.excerpt: For home and working cooks who want one skill done properly.
posts.content:
Our evening course on stocks and sauces runs for six evenings in the teaching kitchens. You make a white and a brown stock, the five classical mother sauces and two reductions, and taste each one with an instructor beside you.

The course costs €480 and does not require a trial day. Places are limited to twelve, the same ratio as the diploma kitchen.

posts.title: School closed over the winter holiday
posts.excerpt: Office and The Pass pause for two weeks at the turn of the year.
posts.content:
The school office and The Pass close for two weeks over the winter holiday. Applications sent in that time are read on our return, and the 1 December deadline for the February intake is not affected.

Term I students will have their next day at 06:30 on the first Monday after the break.
